fullText:
Christa Pike remains unconscious and critically ill after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her last week, her lawyer said, and doctors do not yet know whether she will recover.

"We don't know the prognosis and may not know for several days," attorney Stephen Ferrell said on CNN's State of the Union. Ferrell said he has not been allowed to see her and doesn't know of her speaking or regaining consciousness.

"I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," Ferrell added. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her."

On Monday, Ferrell reiterated his calls to CBS Mornings, saying: "The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her." He said it was not clear when Pike would be able to participate in any legal process were she to recover.

The failed execution led to Gov. Bill Lee announcing on Saturday that Tennessee's top prison official is stepping down.

In a statement, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada said resigning was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" while an independent review examines what happened on Sept. 30, when Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital.

Strada said he still believes the state "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol."

Strada will leave at the end of October, and an interim commissioner will be named later, Lee said.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation "is justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now." "What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement, according to ABC News.

Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996, was unconscious, intubated and breathing with help from a ventilator at a Nashville-area hospital as of Oct. 1, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday. Hospital staff were trying to save her life and flush the pentobarbital from her system, the filing said.

Pike, 50, remained alive and snoring loudly after being given two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys and other witnesses said. She was subsequently taken to a hospital.

Both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at the hospital, her lawyers wrote. They believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

The filing asks a state court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence from the execution attempt.

"Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel, and it was torturous," attorney Randy Spivey said the day after the execution attempt. "It was also predictable."

Spivey said Pike's legal team warned the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical condition of thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." They said it could increase clotting and pain during the execution process and that her veins are difficult to access. Pike's attorneys said the state and the court dismissed their client's concerns.

In audio recordings obtained by the New York Times, Pike had said two weeks before she was due to be executed that she was concerned about the lethal injection, citing a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee of Tony Carruthers in May, when staff were unable to locate a vein. "Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare," Pike can be heard saying in the audio, which was shared by her lawyers.

"I do not have good veins,' she said. "And I don't want to go through that."

"She was not seeking to delay her execution," attorney Stephen Ferrell told reporters on Oct. 1. "She was seeking to have that execution performed humanely and as quickly and as painlessly as possible."

Following the failed execution, Lee ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and said that another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 later this year had been paused.

"This is a tragedy," he said. "There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen. It's deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state."

Pike's attorneys said in response that the governor's independent review doesn't go far enough after being in solitary confinement for more than 20 years and the botched execution attempt. "Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty," Spivey said. "The governor must commute Christa's sentence now.

May Martinez, the mother of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, told NBC News the execution attempt had been a "mess," adding, "They didn't say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. We didn't know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn't work ... and she's on her way to the hospital."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Tennessee should look at other forms of execution. "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," she told The Associated Press.

Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, or explained what went wrong.

Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported. Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defense team, told the BBC it is "very possible" she suffered a brain injury because resuscitation was delayed.

Pike's lawyers have asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt.

President Trump questioned how the execution could have failed, telling reporters it "shouldn't be very difficult," according to AFP. United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk urged Tennessee not to try again.

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for killing Slemmer in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7:54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?"

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper on Wednesday night, "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

A source told NBC News that there was no medical oxygen or mask in the execution chamber, meaning they had to be brought in from a prison clinic. Some of the medication had worn off by the third time staff checked on Pike, the source added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.

According to legal documents filed with the Supreme Court, Pike "tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer" on Jan. 12, 1995 because Pike "just felt mean that day." Pike is reported to have cut Colleen's throat multiple times and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.

Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

Strada took over Tennessee's Department of Correction in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of Arizona's prison system. In late 2024, he announced Tennessee would switch to a single execution drug, pentobarbital.

Death penalty lawyers told the Guardian that Pike's was the fifth "botched" execution Strada has overseen in two states since 2022. That count includes Tennessee's failed attempt to execute Tony Carruthers in May, when staff couldn't find a vein, and three 2022 executions in Arizona in which teams struggled to place IV lines.

Kit Thomas, a death row attorney, told the Guardian that training requirements for execution teams were loosened under Strada. "He reduced the training requirements and we've seen disastrous results," Thomas said.

A day before announcing the resignation, Lee defended the department, telling reporters, "So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined."

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), there were 75 botched lethal injections between 1982 and 2010. Compared to other methods, lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate. There have been a number of botched executions since 2010 that don't appear in the DPIC's tally.

Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. But there are seven known instances in which an execution failed entirely. One of them was earlier this year in Tennessee, when staff were unable to find a vein to administer the lethal drugs to inmate Tony Carruthers.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air, heaving and coughing, convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

In April 2022, Tennessee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug: pentobarbital.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right.

Difficulties with lethal injections have led some states to revive previously discarded execution methods. South Carolina carried out three executions by firing squad last year. There had been three total firing squad executions in the U.S. in the previous half-century combined.

There were 47 executions in 2025, according to the DPIC, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman, who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black, who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.

title: Iran-linked threat prompted U.S. to move bombers from U.K., Trump says
description:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase. 
   The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week, five British ‌men were arrested near the base — which Iran's Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target — on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. 
   "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why ‌would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them," Trump told reporters on Monday.
fullText:
LONDON/WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase.

The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week, five British ‌men were arrested near the base — which Iran's Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target — on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

"We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why ‌would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them," Trump told reporters on Monday. "So we had a threat, and if we're going to be threatened, we just move them, and that sort of alleviates that. And we actually know the people ​that made the threat."

When asked if they were linked to Iran, Trump responded: "They would be linked to Iran."

Earlier on Monday, Vice President JD Vance said the US moved the bombers out of an abundance of caution.

"We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they're trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States (and others), so we are being extremely cautious, and that's all I'd say about that," Vance told reporters.

However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot. He said the Pentagon is "constantly reallocating resources where ‌they need to be."

A NATO military source had said on Monday: "It is still ⁠believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK."

While much about the incident remains unexplained, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any plot was likely backed by Iran.

Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any plot are baseless, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi wrote on X: "I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed ⁠terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree."

Rubio said on Monday the US had confidence in the security of all its bases.

Fairford, located 90 miles (145 km) west of London, is one of the most important European bases for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B-1 aircraft. It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the Middle East, although its ​bombers ​are not stationed there permanently.

During the current conflict, the US had permission to use Fairford only to strike Iranian missile sites ​that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, or so-called defensive strikes. London had ‌refused permission for the US to use British bases for offensive strikes on Iran.

That approach has strained ties between the US and Britain, typically one of Washington's closest allies.

A Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday that all US bombers that had been deployed to Fairford had headed to their home stations in the US.

The Pentagon said the US bomber force remained ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities "anywhere, anytime".

The New York Times, citing two US officials, said the US had rushed over the weekend to move the bombers after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. It said some of the planes had left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled.

A US official declined to comment. The British government also declined to comment, although a spokesman for Burnham said the base was safe.

Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the ‌short term reduce US capacity "to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat".

But he noted that use of Fairford ​was already limited given London's stipulation on defensive strikes. The aircraft could now potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in ​the Gulf, to reduce the need for more air-to-air refuelling to cover the additional distance, but ​that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, he added.

TRUMP SAID PLOT WAS FOR 'BIG DAMAGE'

In the early hours of September 27, five British men in their 20s ‌were arrested after being seen running into fields from three white vans parked near ​the base. Police said no explosive devices were found ​but a quantity of petrol was present.

The men have since been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail.

Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had planned "big damage" and that it might have been connected to Iran. Trump later said he would not have released the ​suspects on bail.

A senior NATO military official said the removal of the bombers would ‌have no impact on the alliance: "NATO's defensive agility towards any aggression remains unchanged and unmatched thanks to the unity, strength, and combined capabilities of 32 nations."

The Wall Street Journal first reported ​the removal of the US bombers.

title: Multiple countries consider restrictions on smart glasses amid privacy concerns
description:
Governments, courts and companies are considering restrictions and examining existing rules on smart glasses amid worries that the technology, ‌brought to mainstream by Meta's Ray-Bans, could be used to photograph, film or ‌audio-record confidential materials or people without their knowledge. 
   Here is a summary of what countries and regions ​are doing to protect people's privacy, in alphabetical order. 
   AUSTRALIA 
   The federal government said in September it was considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces due to privacy and security concerns. 
   Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher asked the country's Public ‌Service Commission for advice on ⁠whether their use should be prohibited and what exemptions might be required. 
   BRITAIN 
   Courts in England and Wales have prohibited the use ⁠of Meta smart glasses because of restrictions on taking images and videos in courts.
fullText:
Oct 6 (Reuters) - Governments, courts and companies are considering restrictions and examining existing rules on smart glasses amid worries that the technology, ‌brought to mainstream by Meta's Ray-Bans, could be used to photograph, film or ‌audio-record confidential materials or people without their knowledge.

Here is a summary of what countries and regions ​are doing to protect people's privacy, in alphabetical order.

The federal government said in September it was considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces due to privacy and security concerns.

Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher asked the country's Public ‌Service Commission for advice on ⁠whether their use should be prohibited and what exemptions might be required.

Courts in England and Wales have prohibited the use ⁠of Meta smart glasses because of restrictions on taking images and videos in courts.

British cinema operators are also introducing policies to prohibit or restrict camera-enabled smart glasses, the ​UK ​Cinema Association said in August.

Smart glasses ​have attracted scrutiny from European privacy ‌regulators and some lawmakers, and the European Data Protection Board has commissioned a report into their "social acceptability".

Member of the European Parliament Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová also urged the European Commission, which has not proposed legislation specifically targeting smart glasses, to consider possible action.

The government said it planned to propose a temporary ban on the ‌use of AI glasses in places where the ​public regularly gather, such as parks, beaches, museums, ​shopping centres and public events.

Norway's ​capital Oslo banned smart glasses in schools in August.

New ‌York's Unified Court System banned smart glasses ​from all its ​court facilities from July 20. The rule covers prescription and non-prescription eyewear or headwear containing cameras, microphones, computers or other technology capable of recording ​video or audio. Visitors ‌carrying them must hand them over to court personnel for safekeeping ​before entering.

title: Trump uses anti-trans slur against Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina
description:
Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews speaks at the Spratt Issues Conference in Florence, S.C., on Aug. 22. (Sean Rayford / Getty)
President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen.
fullText:
President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

In a Truth Social post, Trump referred to Democratic candidate Annie Andrews three times as “trannie.” He said Andrews, who is not transgender, is “not for South Carolina.”

“And South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her,” Trump added.

Andrews responded by largely ignoring the insult, saying in a statement first shared with NBC News that she will “work with anyone to put South Carolina first.”

“As a mom and a pediatrician, I’m in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids, and South Carolina,” Andrews said, adding that “lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together.”

“If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said.

Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the post by Trump, who often uses insulting nicknames for politicians and officials he dislikes.

Reached for comment on why Trump used the slur, the White House referred NBC News to his social media post.

The Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ advocacy organization, blasted Trump’s remarks, calling them “the sad, disgusting, pathetic diatribes of a lame duck president with record-low approvals.”

“So low, in fact, he’s having to campaign in deep red territory in a desperate attempt to shore up support ahead of the midterms,” Ramiro Sarmiento, a spokesperson for the organization, said in a statement.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., condemned Trump’s words Monday night, calling his attacks on Andrews “despicable.”

“Annie Andrews is a mom and pediatrician who’s always put her community first — and she’s exactly who South Carolina needs representing them in the Senate,” Schumer said on X.

Andrews, a physician, has previously said she does not support gender-affirming surgery for minors or transgender athletes’ participating in women’s sports.

Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley, a Republican, criticized the president for his attack on Andrews, asking voters to “reject politics based on division and hate.”

“This is abhorrent. Elections don’t have to be about cruelty and lies. South Carolina deserves better,” Beasley wrote Monday night on X.

Graham is running to keep her seat after Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fill her late brother’s seat after Lindsey Graham died in July.

Graham won the Republican primary in a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman by nearly 5 percentage points. She has leaned heavily on Trump’s endorsement to make her case to South Carolina.

While South Carolina has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly three decades, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race toward Democrats last month, moving it from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”

title: Jim Bakker, televangelist who built a massive empire before scandal, dies at 86
description:
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.
Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.
“He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” she said.
fullText:
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.

Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said.

The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show "The Jim Bakker Show" there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.

Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.

When it hit its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.

The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.

Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.

At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.

Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.

Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.

The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.

Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary.

title: Republicans pour $700 million into midterms as red states turn competitive
description:
President Donald Trump arrives to speak at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, on Sunday. (Mark Schiefelbein / AP)
Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts.
Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.
By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month.
fullText:
Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts.

Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.

The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. That’s led by a massive, late investment in the Senate race in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico is threatening a longtime Republican seat and the GOP has poured in almost $150 million in new ad dollars to back up its nominee, Ken Paxton.

The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP.

Democrats still have a number of advantages in their corner, including President Donald Trump and his party’s eroding standing among voters, Democrats’ own well-funded candidates, and help from outside groups. Candidates can take advantage of a rule that allows them to buy television ads at cheaper rates than outside groups, too.

But the color of the outside money flood shows how Republicans, increasingly on defense in both the House and the Senate, are able to lean on their financial advantage in hope of defying political gravity, as party bastions like Texas and even Kansas look more competitive than usual.

“With the environment not on our side and an incumbent presidency, the three things we have going for us are good candidates, a good map and a lot more money than they do,” said a Republican strategist involved in Senate races.

Everything about the late flood of ad spending is bigger in Texas, where a new group called Texas PAC has booked more than $115 million over the last month alone aimed at boosting Paxton, the state attorney general. Democrats haven’t won a statewide election in Texas in more than 30 years.

But because Republicans are spending largely through outside groups, they have to pay a premium on the rates for each ad, while Talarico’s flush campaign is able to capitalize on those lower candidate ad rates. That means the spending disparity is greater than the actual number of ad airings or their reach.

Senate races in Ohio and Michigan also drew more than $75 million in new ad dollars in September, mostly from Republican-aligned groups. They include a super PAC funded by cryptocurrency interests, Trump’s aligned super PACs and other groups aligned with the national party or Senate Republican leadership.

Again, both states have Democratic candidates — former Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio and former county health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — who have been spending significant money on their advertising campaigns.

No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have made more than $150 million in new ad bookings since the start of September across dozens of races. While the groups haven’t confirmed where they’ve gotten their war chest from, The New York Times recently confirmed that MAGA Inc., Trump’s main super PAC, is primarily funding the effort with the hundreds of millions of dollars it has banked over the last few years.

Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, chair of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, touted the party’s spending advantage as key to helping Republicans hold on to their majority and credited Trump’s deep-pocketed political operation with ensuring the flood of cash continues.

Scott told reporters that he met last week with Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and that the message from Wiles was “money will not be our problem.”

“That’s exciting news to me,” Scott said, adding later, “Knowing that they are going to invest completely in these races is incredibly helpful, because cash is king.”

“We finally find ourselves at a cash advantage because of MAGA Inc. It’s a powerful tool that is providing us with the firepower necessary to really share our message,” he said.

Democrats take some solace in where the new spending is going. The vast majority is plowing into states and seats Trump carried in 2024, including congressional districts Trump would have won by double digits that year, like North Carolina’s 1st District, Texas’ 35th District and Alaska’s at-large congressional district.

The money is also going to races in which Republicans felt comfortable until recently, like the Senate race in Kansas, where the top Senate Republican super PAC just reallocated millions initially meant to be spent in North Carolina.

“The money is not because there is this swell of Republican momentum; the money is because of a swell of Republican panic,” said Lauren French, the communications director at Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership. “Voters don’t like anything they are selling — that includes the message, the candidates and the president.”

Meredith Kelly, a longtime Democratic strategist who works on House and Senate races, said, “When you are defending in such deep-red territory, the technical term for that is: ‘You’re f---ed.’”

“Republicans, if they have one advantage, it’s that they have more money, and they are putting that money to the test right now post-Labor Day,” Kelly added. “However, the big question is: Is that money enough to counteract the fact that Donald Trump’s coalition is falling apart?”

Still, Democrats are uncomfortable watching their party get outspent to such a degree.

“It’s a huge problem, and it will be an ongoing problem, and you see all the lists of high-value donors for both parties and we get swamped every time,” Kelly said. “It creates such an initial advantage for the Republicans that we have to close the gap on in a variety of ways — candidate money, better message, better candidates. We are setting ourselves up for an uphill battle every single time because of the Republican donor strength in terms of the billionaire class.”

title: Russia says no plague cases detected among contacts of deceased lab worker
description:
Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among people who had come ‌into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died ‌last week. 
   Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ​a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump. 
   Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 ‌days and that extensive testing ⁠had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work. 
   Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, ⁠where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said that what she called "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed. 
   She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as ​a ​precaution had already been released.
fullText:
MOSCOW, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among people who had come ‌into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died ‌last week.

Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ​a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump.

Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 ‌days and that extensive testing ⁠had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work.

Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, ⁠where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said that what she called "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.

She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as ​a ​precaution had already been released. Local media ​said around 200 people had previously ‌been quarantined.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it.

"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters.

He said the public health watchdog was handling the situation and would provide further information as it became available.

Trump ‌on Monday described the situation as a "big problem ​for Russia". US Secretary of State Marco ​Rubio said on Tuesday it was ​incumbent on Moscow to share more information.

World Health Organization spokesperson ‌Christian Lindmeier said on Tuesday that Russian ​authorities had yet to ​officially respond to a WHO request for information about the death of the lab worker.

"All of the patient's contacts have been reportedly identified and ​are being monitored for illness, ‌and none to date have shown symptoms of illness," he said.

President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them.

While he dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he said he had decided to run them on his own dime rather than that of the U.S. government in a post on his social media platform.

"I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC.

The move comes after the U.S. government bankrolled a series of ads that aired nationally and heavily featured the president. One of the ads was a direct copy of a spot Trump's campaign ran in 2024.

A White House official confirmed to ABC News Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for ads moving forward but defended them as something previous administrations have used.

"Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance defended using taxpayer money to run the ads, claiming they are "public service announcements."

"They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said.

Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies.

"You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said.

"Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said.

Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates.

The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television.

A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort.

Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law.

Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country."

Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history."

The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed.

The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia.

title: White Sox surge past Guardians 4-3 to take 2-0 lead in ALDS and move within 1 win of ALCS
description: The Chicago White Sox defeat the Cleveland Guardians to take a 2-0 series lead in the ALDS.
fullText:
CLEVELAND — The White Sox are returning to Chicago one win from advancing to the American League Championship Series for the first time in 21 years.

Braden Montgomery lined a two-run double down the right-field line in the sixth inning for the go-ahead runs and Sean Burke allowed one hit in 5 1/3 innings of impressive relief as the White Sox rallied past the Cleveland Guardians 4-3 on Monday to take a 2-0 lead in their AL Division Series.

Game 3 is Wednesday afternoon at Guaranteed Rate Field, where the White Sox have two chances to do something they haven't done since 1906 — clinch a postseason series at home.

"They've been waiting 120 years, so maybe we can do it this year," said Grant Taylor, who worked 1 1/3 innings and allowed one hit as he got his second straight save. "I think it's going to be unbelievable. Those fans deserve it. They've been with us for three years of 100 losses and they've been with us a good bit this year giving us a lot of support as we've gone through this. So being able to give them a postseason game is going to be pretty special."

The surprising White Sox improved to 4-0 in these playoffs — all on the road — and are one win from reaching the ALCS for the first time since winning the World Series in 2005. Chicago became the first team to reach the postseason after three straight 100-loss seasons, including a post-1900 record 121 defeats in 2024.

"Our club has been confident the entire year, regardless of the previous result," manager Will Venable said. "They come in ready to play and turn the page. Now, we're really excited to get playoff baseball to our fans."

Munetaka Murakami hit an RBI single in the fourth to get Chicago within 2-1. Chase Meidroth added an RBI single to extend the lead to 4-2.

Jo Adell hit an RBI triple in the eighth and Chase DeLauter had two hits for the Guardians.

Gavin Williams struck out 11, tied for second-most by a Cleveland pitcher in a postseason game. But the offense failed to produce for the second straight game.

"We have had two-game stretches like this all year and we come right back. I've got a lot of faith in this offense. I have a lot of faith in this team," Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. "We've got our work cut out for us. Like I said, this team plays its best with its back against the wall."

The White Sox went ahead with a three-run sixth.

Miguel Vargas led off with a base hit to chase Williams and advanced to second on a groundout. Randal Grichuk drew a walk before a wild pitch by losing pitcher Erik Sabrowski with Tommy Pham at the plate advanced the runners to second and third. Pham flied out to shallow left before Montgomery jumped on a first-pitch fastball to drive in the go-ahead runs.

Montgomery celebrated at second base before scoring on Meidroth's single to right.

"I was just ready for something to attack, and I was ready for his hardest stuff. I gave myself my best chance to succeed," Montgomery said. "I can't even describe how it felt. It's exhilarating. I was just taking it all in."

Burke came on with one out in the third. After Travis Bazzana walked with one out in the fourth, the right-hander retired 13 straight batters until DeLauter got a base hit to end Burke's night.

Burke struck out six and threw 83 pitches, including 53 strikes, to earn the win.

"I was able to settle in and find my groove," Burke said. "I've had openers before, but not in this situation, so I talked with a lot of guys. It's just normal baseball when you get into that game."

Taylor entered and allowed an RBI triple to Adell before Nathaniel Lowe flied out to end the eighth.

After getting shut out Saturday, the Guardians struck quickly with a pair of runs in the first.

Steven Kwan led off with a single and José Ramírez walked before Chase DeLauter's grounder off opener Anthony Kay moved the runners to second and third. Sean Newcomb came on and intentionally walked Adell to load the bases. Lowe hit a high chopper to drive in Kwan, but Newcomb threw it wide of the bag at first, allowing Ramírez to score on the error.

It marked the first time in four games this postseason the White Sox were behind.

Kay faced three batters and threw 17 pitches, including eight strikes.

Williams didn't allow a hit until Kyle Teel led off the fourth with a single.

The right-hander allowed two runs and four hits in five-plus innings. He had eight strikeouts in the first three innings and became the first Cleveland pitcher to strike out five straight in a postseason game.

title: LIV Golf, BC Partners file restructuring support agreement in bankruptcy case
description: Late Monday, the long-awaited restructuring support agreement between LIV Golf and BC Partners was filed in the league’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy case.
fullText:
Late Monday, the long-awaited restructuring support agreement between LIV Golf and BC Partners was filed in the league's Chapter 11 bankruptcy case.

The agreement features a $300 million investment by BC into LIV Golf 2.0, which league CEO Scott O'Neil said would feature a scaled-back schedule and a more "disciplined" approach. The RSA also extends the deadline for current LIV Golf players to commit to the restructured league to Oct. 25.

According to LIV Golf's term sheet with BC Partners, which was a part of Monday's filing, players would receive equity in the restructured league as well as signing bonuses and "certain NIL [name, image and likeness] rights." According to the term sheet, "go-forward player ownership will equal 52.5 percent" of LIV Golf 2.0. That would leave 45 percent equity to BC Partners and any minority investors and 2.5 percent equity to management.

"We believe deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players," O'Neil said in a statement. "We're delivering on our major milestones, and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers."

In August at LIV Golf's season finale, O'Neil referenced the need for a "critical mass" of current players to sign on to version 2.0 but didn't give specifics. While generally he was likely referencing a mixture of stars, like Bryson DeChambeau who has been supportive of the league's next chapter, and lesser-known players, there is also legal element to that number.

According to bankruptcy law, for Chapter 11 restructuring to occur at least two-thirds of the voting creditors from at least 50 percent of the total claims must approve of the restructuring plan. In the case of LIV Golf, the players who are still owed money under existing deals would likely be moved to their own class of creditors, apart from the various vendors who are also a part of the bankruptcy.

Amid LIV bankruptcy case, Sergio Garcia files to terminate contract with league

Sergio Garcia is seeking an exit from his contract with LIV Golf amid the league's Chapter 11 bankruptcy case in New Jersey.

It remains to be seen which players will remain with LIV Golf. Last week, Sergio Garcia submitted a six-page filing in the bankruptcy case asking for clarity regarding the Spaniard's agreement with LIV Golf. "Termination of the agreement is consistent with [LIV Golf's] statement that the agreement is 'not part of [LIV Golf's] go forward business plan' and, accordingly, should not be objectionable to [LIV Golf]," the filing read.

LIV Golf would also have to present a business plan that was considered feasible for the bankruptcy to be approved.

A second-day hearing is scheduled for Wednesday in the New Jersey bankruptcy court but that, according to various sources, will largely be procedural.

If approved by the court at a hearing scheduled for Oct. 14, the RSA will allow LIV Golf to start engaging with key partners — players, sponsors, media partners — regarding a potential go-forward relationship with LIV Golf 2.0. The league could also start preparing for 2027, which O'Neil said would feature 10 events with five tournaments in the United States and five international team events.

title: Red Sox's Craig Breslow Responds to Ben Rice and Cam Schlittler Criticism
description: The Red Sox did what they had to do for the two Yankees' stars.
fullText:
Red Sox's Craig Breslow Responds to Ben Rice and Cam Schlittler Criticism originally appeared on NESN. 

The Boston Red Sox have been impacted by two guys from their backyard, so to say, who are now with the New York Yankees in Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice.

Arguably the best pitcher in all of Major League Baseball, Schlittler played his college days at Northeastern.

Rice, one of the better offensive players in baseball over the past six months, is a New England guy as well. Ultimately, both players would look great in a Red Sox uniform and do a lot for the organization, but there's more to it than the Red Sox missing out on two guys who happened to grow up close to Fenway Park.

At the end of the day, the Red Sox and other teams in Major League Baseball didn't do what was needed to land both of them, and as a result, they're worse off.

The Yankees are the one team out of 29 others that did the right thing in this regard, but similar to every other team in baseball, New York has certainly missed on a lot of other players as well.

According to the latest report, the Red Sox scouted Rice and Schlittler during the draft process, but Craig Breslow responded on Monday morning in a perfect way, perhaps quieting some of the noise from frustrated fans.

"Ray Fagnant, who scouts New England for the Red Sox, recommended both players, but the team passed," the Boston Globe reported.

"I can't speak specifically about Schlittler or Rice. I wasn't here during their drafts. I think there are probably 28 other teams who are saying the exact same thing and what is most important is that we're taking steps to understand how do players like slip through the draft, slip past us, and make sure that when the next player with that ability, is in our backyard, we're taking every opportunity to make sure that they end up in a Red Sox uniform," Breslow said.

While the idea of having Schlittler and Rice in Boston is the right one, it's important to look at context here.

Neither of these guys were marquee prospects, big-time high school recruits, or even great players at every stage of their college careers.

The Red Sox weren't working with some Buster Posey, Stephen Strasburg, or Bryce Harper-caliber player in their backyard. If they were, another team would have selected them before them anyway.

It's easy to look back on what could have been, but truthfully, the same can be said for every team in Major League Baseball, especially the Yankees, who haven't made all the right decisions in their scouting department as well.

title: Jake Oettinger posts a shutout as the Stars beat the Sharks 5-0
description: — Jake Oettinger stopped 14 shots and earned his 17th career shutout as the Dallas Stars beat the San Jose Sharks 5-0 on Monday night for their first victory of the season.The Sharks were without star center Macklin Celebrini, who was scratched a few minutes before the start of the game due to a lower-body injury.
fullText:
DALLAS (AP) — Jake Oettinger stopped 14 shots and earned his 17th career shutout as the Dallas Stars beat the San Jose Sharks 5-0 on Monday night for their first victory of the season.

The Sharks were without star center Macklin Celebrini, who was scratched a few minutes before the start of the game due to a lower-body injury.

Jamie Benn had a goal and an assist, and Miro Heiskanen, Joel Kiviranta, Jason Robertson and Mikko Rantanen also scored for Dallas.

Heiskanen's goal on a backhand shot with 1:09 left in the first period proved to be the winner.

Yaroslav Askarov had 21 saves for the Sharks.

Celebrini, who was recently named San Jose's captain, took part in warmups but left the ice earlier than usual.

Former Stars forward Ty Dellandrea made his season debut in place of Celebrini, the 20-year-old face of the franchise who assisted on Igor Chernyshov's overtime goal Saturday that made San Jose 2-0.

Celebrini over the summer signed a five-year, $94 million extension.

TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Pontus Holmberg and Ilya Mikheyev each had a goal and assist, Andrei Vasilevskiy stopped 13 shots to move into a tie for 20th place on the NHL career wins list, and Tampa Bay beat Philadelphia.

Vasilevskiy's 372nd victory moved him into a tie with Andy Moog. Vasilevskiy needs two more wins to tie John Vanbiesbrouck for 19th place.

Brayden Point and Brandon Hagel also scored for the Lightning, who have won two games since an opening-night loss to the New York Rangers.

Tyson Foerster scored for Philadelphia and Dan Vladar finished with 32 saves.

The Flyers are winless (0-2-2) through four games to start the season for the first time since 2013-14. Philadelphia has been held to two or fewer goals in all four games.

Point scored his first goal of the season with a deflection off a wrist shot from John Carlson at 16:05 of the first period. Holmberg scored 17 seconds into the second period off the rush for a 2-0 lead.

Foerster wheeled a shot from the top of the left circle that hit Tampa Bay defenseman Charle-Edouard D'Astous in front of the net to bring Philadelphia with one at 7:22.

Mikheyev made it 3-1 with a wraparound with three minutes to play. Hagel added an empty-netter.

Nikita Kucherov picked up two assists and now has 1,128 career points to move past Mike Bossy and Joe Nieuwendyk for 67th place.

BOSTON (AP) — Tim Stutzle had two goals and an assist and goalies Linus Ullmark and Samuel Ersson combined to stop 18 of 19 shots as Ottawa defeated Boston.

Stutzle's multi-point game moved him into sole possession of sixth place for most points in Ottawa history with 413.

Ullmark started in goal for Ottawa, but wasn't on the ice at the start of the third period. The onetime Bruin netminder, who stopped all 10 shots he faced in the first two periods, was on the bench five minutes into the final period. Ersson made eight saves in the final period for the Senators.

Ottawa's Michael Amadio had a goal and assist, and Drake Batherson also scored.

Boston rookie James Hagan spoiled Ottawa's shutout bid with a goal in the third period. Jeremy Swayman made 20 saves for the Bruins, who have lost two straight after opening the season with two wins.

Boston was outshot 24-19 and failed to score on four power plays.

PITTSBURGH (AP) — Alex Iafallo had a goal and an assist, Clay Stevenson made 29 saves, and Winnipeg beat Pittsburgh.

Pittsburgh's Declan Carlile scored 8:53 into the third period to tie the game at 2-2, but Cole Perfetti scored the winner on a wrist shot just nine seconds later, assisted by Josh Morrissey, to put the Jets ahead to stay.

Adam Lowry also scored for the Jets, who have won two in a row after losing their season opener.

Benjamin Kindel also scored for the Penguins and Carlile added an assist. Sergei Murashov made 30 saves for the Penguins.

The Jets outhit the Penguins by 12, 23 to 11.

title: New Orleans Pelicans With Most To Gain From Strong Preseason
description: The New Orleans Pelicans kick off their preseason on Tuesday night. Here are the players with the most to gain from a strong batch of games.
fullText:
The New Orleans Pelicans kick off their preseason on Tuesday night against the Oklahoma City Thunder, allowing a look at what this squad is going to look like this season under new coach Jamahl Mosley and his staff.

While most of the excitement will be from how the starters look together and what this defense looks like, there are also a couple of people who need to use this opportunity to make an impact.

Here are the Pelicans who have the most to gain from a strong batch of games before the regular season begins:

Poole is someone who could help transform this team. He is an NBA champion who scored 18.5 points per game on that team. New Orleans hasn't gotten that Golden State Warriors version of him, though.

The 27-year-old was clearly not a fit for whatever the Pelicans had going on, when combined with him battling injuries, it was an ugly year that saw him out of the rotation at times. He posted 13.4 points, 2.0 rebounds and 3.1 assists per night on 37.2/33.3/86.0 shooting splits.

Poole has a chance to start over with this new staff and remind people of what he can do. He'll need to do that to in order to win minutes back with Dejounte Murray and Jeremiah Fears both firmly ahead of him at that guard spot.

Johnson is likely entering a contract year with a looming $5 million option for next year that the team would have to accept before the end of the month. Given what happened with Jordan Hawkins, it would be shocking to see them accept it.

That means that the former first-round pick is going to need to make the most of whatever minutes he gets this year, starting with the preseason.

He needs to show that he can consistently hit threes. Right now, he's shooting 24.5% for his career, but he expects far better from himself. Along with that, this staff is going to be looking for defensive effort.

These three are being lumped in together, because they are currently the odd men out on the roster. Trendon Watford's contract doesn't gain it's next guarantee until Opening Day, but he is certainly a favorite to end up making the team. That puts the onus on the others to stand out and show why they should be the choice. They could also show off for their next teams, as well. Like with Johnson, they can't afford to waste any minutes.

fullText:
ARKADELPHIA, Ark. (KLRT) - For the first time since 2021, Henderson State football is 5-0.

The Reddies have put together a perfect start to the season, and head coach Greg Holsworth says the team's hard work throughout the offseason is paying off.

"Feels really good. I can't be better than 5-0 after five games," Holsworth said. "We've been close around here for a long time and all the work these guys put in in the spring, the summer and just being on the sideline being like, let's go, let's go get this thing guys."

Henderson State's latest win was its toughest test yet.

The Reddies held off a gritty Southwestern Oklahoma State team, 38-33, after trailing for the first time entering the fourth quarter this season.

HSU rallied in the final quarter, outscoring the Bulldogs 14-7. Former Bryant quarterback and Razorback baseball player Austin Ledbetter played a key role in helping the Reddies complete the comeback.

Holsworth said he was proud of the way his team responded when the momentum shifted.

"Really, really proud of them," Holsworth said. "At one point they had all the momentum and we just stayed in the fight. Made some big plays on offense, big plays on defense. And just kept battling and kept battling and eventually took that thing over and got the win."

The 5-0 start has also pushed Henderson State into the national rankings.

The Reddies are No. 17 in the latest Division II AFCA Coaches Poll and are one of 15 unbeaten Division II teams remaining in the country.

But despite the strong start, Holsworth knows his team still has plenty to improve on.

"Focus on the little details. We got a lot to improve on, okay? And in this game showed it," Holsworth said. "Short term negatives turned into long term positives. We messed some stuff up, but you can fix it and get better down the road."

Henderson State will look to make it six straight wins Saturday when the Reddies travel to face Northwestern Oklahoma State.

The Reddies are off to their best start in five years, but they know the bigger goals are still ahead.

title: Guardians' bats go cold again, wasting Gavin Williams' 11 strikeouts in Game 2 loss
description: — The Cleveland Guardians have picked a bad time for their offense to go cold again.Manager Stephen Vogt's squad had one of the worst offenses in the American League before turning it on after the Aug.
fullText:
CLEVELAND (AP) — The Cleveland Guardians have picked a bad time for their offense to go cold again.

Manager Stephen Vogt's squad had one of the worst offenses in the American League before turning it on after the Aug. 3 trade deadline en route to winning its third straight AL Central title.

The offensive surge hasn't carried into the postseason.

Cleveland had only four hits in Monday's 4-3 loss to the Chicago White Sox in Game 2 of their AL Division Series. The Guardians managed just three hits in Saturday's 3-0 loss.

The Guardians had a .231 batting average before the trade deadline, second-worst in the American League. But from Aug. 3 until the end of the regular season, they batted .255, which ranked third.

They don't have much time to get things back on track, with Game 3 on Wednesday in Chicago as Cleveland tries to avoid getting swept in a Division Series for the first time since 2018 against Houston.

"I think we've done a really good job of flushing games. Have the day off tomorrow, make sure we have some good focus, but obviously, yeah, not how you wanted to finish Game 2," outfielder Steven Kwan said.

It is only the fourth time since Division Series started in 1995 that a team has had seven or fewer hits over the first two games. The others were the 2008 Milwaukee Brewers, 2010 Cincinnati Reds (who were no-hit by Philadelphia in Game 1) and 2018 Cleveland Indians.

Cleveland's leadoff hitter has reached base only twice in the two games and the team is 0 for 8 with runners in scoring position.

The White Sox going with bullpen games in the first two games of the series has also put Cleveland hitters off balance.

"They made great pitches and we battled and we haven't given any at-bats away. And I think the name of the game is, `Who Lands a Pitch?' And when they made those mistakes, we just weren't able to capitalize maybe in the way we wanted to, but that's part of the game," outfielder Jo Adell said.

Adell gave Cleveland some fleeting hope in the eighth with an RBI triple to get the Guardians within one run. But then Nathaniel Lowe flied out to end the inning.

"We put good swings up (in the late innings) and I think that's what we're capable of," Adell said. "We had a lot of those balls that, mine included, I for sure though it was out and it's one of those days where it didn't travel that way and that's the way the game is. But we're convicted in our approach and our at-bats and we have a bunch of really good players in here, so we're going to continue to fight."

Cleveland's struggles on offense wasted a strong start from Gavin Williams, whose 11 strikeouts were tied for second-most in team history in a postseason game.

The right-hander — who led the AL in strikeouts this season — struck out eight in the first three innings and became the first pitcher in franchise history to whiff five straight in a postseason game. He also had 16 pitches over 100 mph, the fourth-most by an AL pitcher in a playoff game since tracking started in 2008.

His 0-2 fastball to Munetaka Murakami in the fourth inning registered 101.2 mph, which was the hardest pitch of his career.

"I feel like I've been doing it all year. It just wasn't today. I know I've hit 101 a couple times this year, but could be the juices, too," Williams said. "I don't think I was too worried about the strikeouts. Just trying to put the team in a good position to win."

Williams — who allowed two runs and four hits — came out in the sixth after allowing a leadoff single to Miguel Vargas. The White Sox scored three times that inning off Erik Sabrowski and Hunter Gaddis to take the lead.

"We couldn't have asked any more from Gavin other than maybe a few more pitches. He did his job and then some. That is a big-time performance by a big-time pitcher," Vogt said.

title: ‘What Are You Talking About?,’ ‘Welcome to Big-Time Sports!’ — Ex-Indiana Coach Tells Kelsey Mitchell to ‘Grow Up’ Amid Caitlin Clark Controversy
description: Indiana Fever star Kelsey Mitchell opened up about the criticism she receives from fans just by playing next to Caitlin Clark. Mitchell admitted this has created difficulties for her, which could influence what she plans to do this offseason.
fullText:
Indiana Fever star Kelsey Mitchell opened up about the criticism she receives from fans just by playing next to Caitlin Clark. Mitchell admitted this has created difficulties for her, which could influence what she plans to do this offseason.

Sportscaster Dan Dakich took exception to Mitchell's comments and did not mince words in calling her out.

Indiana has been at the center of the spotlight over the past few years, largely due to Clark's arrival in 2024.

However, she hasn't just brought increased popularity with her. The 24-year-old has invited scrutiny toward her teammates, which has weighed heavily on Mitchell.

Following the Fever's first-round exit at the hands of the Las Vegas Aces, Mitchell opened up about how fans have treated her.

The 2018 No. 2 pick claimed that people do not understand how difficult it is to be a professional athlete. She went on to frame the scrutiny and criticism she is subjected to as stemming from being Clark's teammate.

"Playing with CC and having the eyes that she got, we get a lot of flak just for being on her team," Mitchell said. "… I just think that people got to give us grace. I think this organization is unbelievable, man, but I think that when it comes to really trying to be yourself, it hasn't always been easy."

Dakich, a former interim coach of the Indiana Hoosiers, responded to Mitchell's comments on "Don't @ Me" on Monday.

"Let's understand something, Kelsey. Sports fans have disliked their own teams ten minutes into the sports being invented," Dakich said.

He then went on to cite various instances of fans going after the players of the teams they support over on-court mistakes.

"Ask an NBA player who misses shot after shot in Game 6, Game 7. I mean, what are you talking about?" Dakich continued. "You want everybody to wake up and go, 'Oh my god, it's a fever fan.' Welcome to big-time sports.

"I mean, you all want big-time sports, as Sophie Cunningham said. And now you [expletive], whine, and moan, and you act coy and cute and all that little [expletive] that you're doing right there because you're getting scrutiny? … Welcome to big-time sports, little girl. Now grow up, be a woman, be an adult."

Mitchell has played nine years in the WNBA, all with the Fever. Prior to Clark's arrival, she was the offensive engine that ran the team.

In the six years before Clark was drafted, she averaged 16.4 points and 3.0 assists per game and was named an All-Star in 2023. However, the team constantly struggled, winning fewer than 10 games in four of those six seasons.

Clark's arrival in 2024 rejuvenated the team. She helped them reach 20 wins for the first time since 2015 in her maiden season. Additionally, that year marked the end of the franchise's seven-year postseason drought.

MORE: 'Most Important Offseason' — ESPN Legend Urges Fever to Bolster Roster Around Caitlin Clark

Mitchell's game also seemed to get elevated by playing alongside Clark. Since 2024, her scoring has increased yearly, and she has earned three straight All-Star nods. This season, she put up a career-high 24.7 points per game.

The backcourt duo of Mitchell and Clark is considered one of the best superstar pairings in the WNBA. However, it could soon be coming to an end.

The four-time All-Star enters the offseason as an unrestricted free agent. Several teams are sure to show interest, especially with Mitchell coming off a career year.

After her telling comments during her season-ending press conference, some believe she will test free agency. If she chooses to sign elsewhere, one of the league's best one-two combos would be abruptly separated before reaching the level of success many expected.

title: Four observations as Yankees now face elimination with ALDS Game 2 loss
description: The Yankees are one loss from elimination. Four key observations and takeaways from their ALDS Game 2 loss to the Rays.
fullText:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - This was the Rays' way, on full display in a pivotal Game 2.

Put the ball in play, use speed and daring on the bases and force the defense - in this case a skittish group of Yankees infielders - to make plays, or mistakes.

Cam Schlittler wasn't at his best Monday night, but the Yankees threatened a franchise postseason record for errors in one game at Tropicana Field, where the Rays own a huge house advantage.

Under the dome and on the spongy artificial surface, the Yankees' 5-2 loss pushed them to the brink elimination as this best-of-five AL Division Series shifts to the Bronx on Wednesday night.

Here are our takeaways from a lost Game 2:

This is where it all unraveled, with a four-run fifth inning that broke open a 1-1 game.

Jonathan Aranda (single) and Junior Caminero (double) opened at second and third. From there, two misplays by rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. led to two runs.

Schlittler was gone after 76 stressful pitches (7 hits, 1 walk, just 2 strikeouts), leading to Richie Palacios' sharp, two-run single off a full-count pitch by Brent Headrick.

Just before that two-out hit made it 5-1, Lombard - with a runner crossing in front of him as he fielded Jonny DeLuca's grounder - rushed a wide throw to first for an error.

The first two runs off Schlittler were the product of soft contact, but highlighted the Rays' ability to pressure a defense with their speed and ability to put the ball in play - even against a pitcher with three different fastballs at high octane who'll be a shoe-in Cy Young Award winner next month.

Both came with the Yanks' infield in.

Liam Hicks' soft bouncer toward second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. took away his play at the plate, settling for the out at first.

Next up, Chandler Simpson, possibly the fastest runner in game, sent a weak grounder to Lombard, who whiffed on a rushed backhanded attempt, looking for a play at the plate.

Originally scored an error, it went as an infield hit and the Rays had a 3-1 lead.

And it could've been even worse.

Tampa Bay led 1-0 after the first, an inning where the Yanks' committed three errors - including a throwing error by second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. that scored the unearned run.

Chisholm's second errant toss cost the Yanks a synch inning-ending double play, but Schlittler picked up his teammates in that 19-pitch frame.

It started with a leadoff error by third baseman Ryan McMahon on Yandy Diaz's grounder and included a would-be third strike erased by Austin Wells' catcher's interference on Liam Hicks.

The Yanks' inability to take care of the ball has been a fundamental issue at times, and it has cost them in postseason, most notably in the decisive World Series Game 5 vs. the Dodgers.

Chisholm's error was a reckless play; he had no shot at doubling up Caminero, who was well across first base as the second baseman's off-balance throw went wild.

Ben Rice's two-homer night gave him four in four postseason games this year.

Leading off the fourth inning against Peralta, the lefty-hitting Rice's game-tying solo home was the Yanks first hit Monday, after being one-hit in Game 1 by Drew Rasmussen and Bryan Baker.

Rice's love affair with the Trop continued with a solo shot in the eighth off lefty Ian Seymour, making Rice a .448 hitter (13-for-29) this year - including postseason - under St. Pete's outdated dome, with seven home runs and 12 RBI.

Of course, we were bound to have some catwalk chaos here too, when Spencer Jones' towering fly to start the second inning struck the B-ring (in play).

But right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. made the catch - which otherwise would've likely been a fly out to center.

Before the game, Yanks manager Aaron Boone said he though about some alteration to his lineup.

But he ultimately felt convicted in running back the same order that was no-hit by Drew Rasmussen into the eighth inning of Game 1.

Once change he could've made was for McMahon, who entered 1-for-14 vs. starter Freddy Peralta, who lasted 4.2 innings.

Yet to see a 2026 postseason at-bat entering Monday, Jose Caballero (0-for-2 career vs. Peralta) was one possible choice.

Anthony Volpe (2-for-4, double, HR career vs. Peralta) was another, but that small sample size, plus Boone's reluctance to play him at third base at the Trop was a factor.

McMahon (0-for-1) did draw a full-count walk that ended Peralta's night in the fifth inning.
